description: I'm a CS–AI student at the University of Alberta, interested in ML, AI and data science. I have experience with Python, SQL and software development, and have worked on data analysis and predictive modelling projects. I'm exploring a wildfire intelligence platform using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS data. Looking for teammates skilled in Python, ML, geospatial analysis, web development or UI/UX who are collaborative and eager to build something impactful!
summary: This weekend we built Ember, an interactive web application that harmonizes two decades of NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire data into a single, continuous record. To address the challenge of harmonizing data from two different satellites, Ember solves the discrepancy caused by the newer VIIRS sensor, which detects far more fires due to its sharper 375-meter resolution compared to MODIS's 1-kilometer resolution. Ember utilizes a spatial machine learning pipeline to calibrate fire energy and translate historical MODIS data into VIIRS terms, putting every year on the same scale. The resulting platform allows users to view accurate trends, anomalies, and fire regimes, alongside 7- and 30-day forecasts. It also features an AI chatbot and accessibility tools, including but not limited to data sonification for visually impaired users. This project is important because the MODIS satellite is retiring in 2027, and without a harmonized bridge, the historical fire data will no longer be comparable to future VIIRS observations. Ember provides fire planners, researchers, and the public with a reliable 20-year baseline, ensuring that historical fire trends remain accurate and free from artificial spikes caused by changing sensor technology.  VIIRS is the future. Ember brings the past with it.
details:
Terra and Aqua, the satellites behind NASA’s 20-year MODIS fire record, retire in 2026-27. Their successor, VIIRS, has a sharper 375 m pixel, sees two to three times more small fires, and measures fire energy differently. Put the two records side by side and 2026 looks like a disaster compared with 2006 even when it isn’t. Ember fixes that. It converts MODIS into VIIRS terms so 2006-2026 reads as one consistent record, then lets anyone explore it for any place on Earth.

Using it
Search a place, type coordinates, or draw a box. Trends gives you one sentence on how this year compares to a usual year, plus a calendar of burning activity (years down, months across). Anomalies flags the months furthest from that area’s normal and gives each a σ score. Patterns groups the planet into 7 fire regimes by clustering 17 features per cell: seasonality, frequency, fire energy, duration, night-time share and re-burns. Forecast predicts hotspots for the next 7 and 30 days with a 5-95% range. Listen plays a fire season as sound, and Speak adds voice commands and read-aloud so the app works without looking at the screen. The app also has a colour-blind palette and an accessibility window. A chat assistant answers questions about whatever place and years are on screen.

The Fire Map shows real hotspots on a NASA satellite basemap and switches between Hotspots, Patterns and Confidence. Confidence shows what MODIS can and can’t tell us at VIIRS scale. It has three views: our estimate of the chance VIIRS sees fire around each MODIS detection (from MODIS alone, using a calibrated CNN ensemble), what VIIRS actually saw, and how unsure the model is. Hover over any cell to see all three plus the model’s average error.

Under the hood
We grid FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP hotspots per 2° cell per month, keeping vegetation fires and dropping low-confidence detections. In the {H} months when both sensors were flying, Ember learns how many VIIRS hotspots and how much VIIRS fire radiative power (FRP) each cell shows per unit of MODIS. Cells with very few fires get ratios that lean on their 10° region and the global average, so a handful of detections can’t produce a wild correction. Real VIIRS months stay as they are, and converted MODIS months are labelled “estimated” in the app.

To understand the sensors at pixel level, we matched 18.9 million MODIS detections to VIIRS within 1 km and 60 minutes. 28% had a VIIRS twin. To estimate where the 375 m fire sits inside a 1 km MODIS pixel, we tried a Random Forest, a CNN, and a U-Net paired with a conditional-GAN discriminator. The calibrated CNN ensemble did best and powers the Confidence layer. For the regimes we compared K-Means (k=7) with HDBSCAN and kept K-Means. The forecast is an XGBoost quantile model that uses recent fire activity, NASA POWER weather and soil moisture, and the time of year.

Does it work?
Every test below used data the models never saw.

Harmonized counts vs. real VIIRS: R² {H} per cell-month, against {H} for raw MODIS. The world monthly total lands within {H}% (raw MODIS: {H}%).
FRP: R² 0.48 per 2° cell-day but only 0.07 per pixel. That gap is why Ember compares areas and never makes claims about single pixels.
Sub-pixel location: on held-out months, the calibrated CNN ensemble scores ROC-AUC 0.62 and Brier 0.174. A constant guess scores 0.180, so the skill is real but modest. That’s why the Confidence layer shows uncertainty with every estimate instead of a single sharp answer.
Forecast, leave-one-year-out across 2006-2025: 7-day error is 17% lower than “repeat last week” and 43% lower than “usual for this date.” 82% of actual values fell inside the predicted range.
Regimes hold steady across random seeds (ARI 0.95) and line up with regions fire scientists already recognize: Canadian boreal, the Amazon arc, and African and Australian savanna.

Why bother
Fire agencies, researchers and reporters keep asking the same question: how does this season compare to normal? Canada’s 2023 season burned about 8x a typical year, and that comparison only holds if every year was counted the same way. Once MODIS goes dark, the baseline stops growing and the new data no longer matches it. Ember keeps the long-term record usable for planning, research and public communication. It’s free, runs in a browser with no login, and needs no GIS skills.

What’s different about it
Most fire tools show one sensor and leave the handover problem to the user. Ember makes the handover the problem it solves, and a MODIS vs. Ember slider shows what harmonization changes. It’s also upfront about its limits. Estimates are labelled, forecasts carry ranges, and the per-pixel model comes with its own uncertainty map instead of pretending to be sharper than it is. Turning a season into sound gives people who don’t read charts, including low-vision users, another way in.

Decisions we made along the way
We converted between sensors instead of stitching the records together, because a hotspot doesn’t mean the same thing on both. We pulled sparse cells toward regional averages so quiet places don’t produce noisy corrections. We tested at pixel, cell and global scale and only make claims at the scales that held up. Forecasts had to beat simple baselines, not just look good. Filtering to vegetation fires keeps gas flares and industrial heat out of the wildfire count. We used only open data, respected every licence, and didn’t generate or modify any NASA branding.

Built with
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet and topojson-client on the front end. Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, HDBSCAN, XGBoost, PyTorch) and FastAPI for data and models. Hosted on GitHub Pages and Cloudflare Workers. NASA data: FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS S-NPP, NASA POWER (MERRA-2), GIBS/Worldview corrected reflectance, MODIS Land Cover (MCD12Q1), and elevation. Google Gemini runs the in-app chatbot. Claude helped write and debug code and draft text, and the team reviewed and tested all of it. No special hardware, just our laptops.
